zh.q: 一堆矿石从炉顶倒下去，为什么出来就是铁水？
zh.concl: 这是一台逆流的还原炉：炉料从上往下、热风从下往上，两边对着跑，才有「上部低温、下部高温」的分级还原。
points: 全厂五个工段：上料 → 高炉本体 → 热风 → 渣铁 → 煤气净化，料和气在本体里对着跑。
顶栏的 Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ 是简化总式，真实过程还分级还原、造渣、渗碳。
逆流是关键：煤气一路往上被消耗、被换热，才形成上部低温、下部高温的温度梯度。

zh.q: 矿石、焦炭、石灰石为什么不能混成一堆，要一层一层地铺？
zh.concl: 分层不是为了好看：焦炭层是料柱的骨架兼透气窗，矿层夹在中间被上升的煤气一层层还原；混成一堆，煤气就穿不动。
points: 上料按「批」：矿批、焦批、熔剂批交替入炉，形成料层。
焦炭要强度高、块度合适、硫磷灰分低，否则被压碎就堵死料柱。
石灰石随矿批加进去，进炉后才分解成 CaO——在上料阶段它还不干活。

zh.q: 同一个炉子里，为什么从上到下不是一处一色？
zh.concl: 五带不是画上去的：温度自炉顶向炉缸递增，每一带只做一件事，所以铁的还原也只能一级一级完成。
points: 块状带占了大半个炉身，是间接还原的主战场。
软熔带（约 1100–1400 ℃）是炉料软化到熔化、初渣形成的区间，它的位置决定料柱透气好坏；石灰石是在它上面的 800–1000 ℃ 先分解成 CaO 的。
风口回旋带 1500–1600 ℃、理论燃烧温度 2000–2300 ℃，是全炉唯一的热源。

zh.q: 焦炭在风口烧出来的是 CO 还是 CO₂？
zh.concl: CO 不是一步烧出来的：焦炭先在风口烧成 CO₂（放热），CO₂ 上升穿过炽热焦炭层被还原成 CO（吸热可逆）——风口是全炉唯一的热源与 CO 的源头。
points: 教材的口径是两步：焦炭在风口先燃烧生成 CO₂（放热），CO₂ 上升穿过炽热的焦炭层再被还原成 CO（吸热）。
这两步合起来，碳过量时的总结果相当于 2C + O₂ → 2CO——但不要因此把教材的 C + O₂ → CO₂ 当成错的。
教材原文还写明：C + CO₂ ⇌ 2CO 是一个可逆反应，并且自下而上发生在有焦炭的地方——这就是炉顶煤气里总有没被利用的 CO 的原因（下一节「尾气之谜」）。

zh.q: CO 一路上升，凭什么把铁从氧化物里一层层剥出来？
zh.concl: 逐级还原：每一级在各自的温度带完成；温度够高的地方再由 C + CO₂ ⇌ 2CO 补 CO（吸热可逆，正好接平衡知识）。
points: 高温区靠 C + CO₂ ⇌ 2CO 把 CO₂ 换回 CO，这是吸热反应，升温有利于生成 CO——接选必 1 的可逆反应（别写成反向的 2CO ⇌ CO₂ + C，那是放热那一侧）。
直接还原与间接还原并存：焦炭既是燃料、又是还原剂、还是料柱骨架。

zh.q: 矿石里的 SiO₂ 是杂质，凭什么能被赶出去？
zh.concl: CaCO₃ 先分解出 CaO（吸热），CaO 再拉走 SiO₂ 变成 CaSiO₃ 液渣浮在铁水上：渣稀了铁水才干净，不加石灰石省了焦却排不掉杂质。
points: 造渣是两步：CaCO₃ 先分解成 CaO（吸热），CaO 再与 SiO₂ 成 CaSiO₃ 液渣，别写成一步。
碱度 R = CaO/SiO₂，窗口 1.0–1.3，对应滑块上 150–210 kg/t 那段带；关掉石灰石不是「没有渣」，是「渣不够碱」。
渣浮在铁水上、从渣口排；铁水从位置更低的铁口出——方向别弄反。

zh.q: 把风温调高一点，真的能省下焦炭吗？
zh.concl: 风温每降 100 ℃，焦比大约多 20 kg/t、产量跟着掉——反过来说提高风温是最直接的省焦手段，代价是热风炉格子砖与风口的承受能力（工业带 1100–1250 ℃）。
points: 风温经「带进显热」直接替换烧掉的焦炭，是本课最便宜的一招。
焦比降了，单位时间的出铁量也跟着升（本课按 产量 ∝ 1/焦比 建模，属课件设定，不是教材规律）。
风温不是越高越好：越 1300 ℃ 风口与围管烧穿，低于 950 ℃ 炉缸热量不足会炉凉。

zh.q: 焦比、碱度、产量同时卡住时，你先动哪一个？
zh.concl: 焦比 ≤ 360 kg/t 把风温压到 ≥ 1150 ℃ 左右，碱度窗口把石灰石锁在 150–210 kg/t，产量还要靠富氧补——可行的是风温 1150–1250 ℃ 这一小片，折中是算出来的。
points: 焦比 ≤ 360 kg/t 把风温压到 ≥ 1150 ℃ 左右，产量缺口靠富氧补。
碱度窗口把石灰石锁在 150–210 kg/t，取多了渣量大、焦比反升。
风温 1300 ℃ 走「风口烧穿」，两条事故链都要看懂。

en.q: Ore is tipped in at the furnace top. Why does molten iron come out?
en.concl: This is a counterflow reduction furnace: charge travels top to bottom and hot blast bottom to top, running against each other, which gives stepwise reduction from a cool top to a hot bottom.
points: Five plant sections: charging → furnace body → hot blast → slag and iron → gas cleaning; charge and gas run against each other inside the body.
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ in the top bar is a simplified overall equation; the real process also involves stepwise reduction, slag formation and carburization.
Counterflow is the key: the gas is consumed and exchanges heat all the way up, creating a gradient that is cool at the top and hot at the bottom.

en.q: Why can't ore, coke and limestone be mixed in one heap, but must be laid down layer by layer?
en.concl: Layering is not for looks: coke layers are the column's skeleton and gas windows, while ore layers sandwiched between are reduced layer by layer by the rising gas; mixed in a heap, the gas cannot get through.
points: Charging is by "batch": ore, coke and flux batches go in turn, forming layers.
Coke must be strong, well sized and low in sulfur, phosphorus and ash; crushed coke chokes the burden column.
Limestone goes in with the ore and decomposes to CaO only inside the furnace; at the charging stage it does no work yet.

en.q: Why does the same furnace look different from top to bottom?
en.concl: The five zones are not just drawn on: temperature rises from top to hearth, each zone does one job, so iron can only be reduced one stage at a time.
points: The lumpy zone fills most of the stack and is the main arena for indirect reduction.

The cohesive zone (about 1100–1400 ℃) is where the burden softens and melts and the first slag forms; its position decides how permeable the burden is. Limestone has already decomposed to CaO above it, at 800–1000 ℃.
The tuyere raceway at 1500–1600 ℃, with a theoretical flame temperature of 2000–2300 ℃, is the furnace's only heat source.

en.q: Does coke burning at the tuyeres give CO or CO₂?
en.concl: CO is not made in one step: coke first burns to CO₂ at the tuyeres (exothermic), and the CO₂ rising through hot coke is reduced to CO (endothermic, reversible); the tuyeres are the furnace's only heat source and the origin of its CO.
points: The textbook gives two steps: coke first burns at the tuyeres to CO₂ (exothermic), then the CO₂ rising through hot coke is reduced to CO (endothermic).
Together, with excess carbon, the net result equals 2C + O₂ → 2CO, but that does not make the textbook's C + O₂ → CO₂ wrong.

The textbook also states that C + CO₂ ⇌ 2CO is reversible and happens from the bottom up wherever there is coke; this is why the top gas always contains unused CO (the next section, "the puzzle of the top gas").

en.q: As CO rises, how does it strip iron out of its oxides layer by layer?
en.concl: Stepwise reduction: each stage is completed in its own temperature zone; where it is hot enough, C + CO₂ ⇌ 2CO replenishes CO (endothermic and reversible, linking neatly to equilibrium).
points: Each reduction stage has its own temperature: 200–700 ℃ → about 850 ℃ → about 1200 ℃.

In the hot zone, C + CO₂ ⇌ 2CO turns CO₂ back into CO; this is endothermic, so higher temperature favors CO, linking to reversible reactions in Elective 1 (don't write it backward as 2CO ⇌ CO₂ + C, which is the exothermic direction).
Direct and indirect reduction coexist: coke is fuel, reducing agent and burden skeleton all at once.

en.q: SiO₂ in the ore is an impurity. How can it be driven out?
en.concl: CaCO₃ first decomposes to CaO (endothermic), then CaO carries SiO₂ away as liquid CaSiO₃ slag floating on the iron: only fluid slag gives clean iron. Skipping limestone saves coke but leaves the impurities in.
points: Slag forms in two steps: CaCO₃ first decomposes to CaO (endothermic), then CaO combines with SiO₂ to form liquid CaSiO₃ slag; don't write it as one step.
Basicity R = CaO/SiO₂ with a window of 1.0–1.3, matching the 150–210 kg/t band on the slider; turning off limestone does not mean "no slag" but "slag not basic enough".
Slag floats on the iron and leaves through the slag notch; iron leaves through the lower taphole. Don't get the directions backward.

en.q: Raise the blast temperature a little. Does it really save coke?
en.concl: Each 100 ℃ drop in blast temperature adds about 20 kg/t of coke and output falls; put the other way, raising blast temperature is the most direct way to save coke, at the cost of what the stove checker bricks and tuyeres can withstand (industrial band 1100–1250 ℃).
points: Blast heat directly replaces burned coke through "sensible heat brought in"; it is the cheapest trick in this lesson.
As the coke rate falls, iron output per unit time rises (this lesson models output ∝ 1/coke rate, a lesson setting, not a textbook law).
Hotter is not always better: above 1300 ℃ tuyeres and the bustle pipe burn through; below 950 ℃ the hearth lacks heat and the furnace chills.

en.q: When coke rate, basicity and output are all stuck, which do you move first?
en.concl: Coke rate ≤ 360 kg/t pushes the blast temperature to about ≥ 1150 ℃, the basicity window locks limestone to 150–210 kg/t, and output still needs oxygen enrichment; the feasible region is a small patch at 1150–1250 ℃, so the compromise is calculated.
points: Coke rate ≤ 360 kg/t pushes the blast temperature to about ≥ 1150 ℃; any output shortfall is made up with oxygen enrichment.
The basicity window locks limestone to 150–210 kg/t; too much gives a lot of slag and the coke rate rises again.
Below 950 ℃ leads to "3 s countdown → hearth freezes", above 1300 ℃ to "tuyere burn-through"; understand both accident chains.
